sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In 1878, James J. Sylvester first coined the term “graph”1. Since then, Graph Theory has developed into a rapidly growing branch of mathematics. It has found widespread applications across numerous fields, including engineering, computer science, biology, operations research, statistical mechanics, optimization theory, physics, and chemistry. One significant branch of this discipline is Chemical Graph Theory, pioneered by researchers such as Milan Randić2, Ante Graovac3, Haruo Hosoya4, Alexander Balaban5, Ivan Gutman6, and Nenad Trinajstić3, which has become a cornerstone of mathematical chemistry.

Topological indices provide valuable insights into the physicochemical properties of chemical compounds7. In cheminformatics, QSPR and QSAR are two important methodologies used to predict the physicochemical behavior of molecules8. These approaches rely heavily on topological indices and contribute significantly to their ongoing investigation9. A molecular graph represents a molecule by associating vertices with atoms and edges with covalent bonds, thereby offering a rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing molecular structures and properties10.

A wide range of research studies have investigated distinct degree-based topological indices for specific families of graphs (11). To overcome the limitations of existing methods, the present study focuses on the use of the M-polynomial, which provides a unified representation of many degree-based indices. Specifically, such indices can often be expressed as derivatives, integrals, or combinations thereof of the corresponding M-polynomial.

Recent advances in chemical graph theory have increasingly employed the M-polynomial approach to explore various chemical structures12. Numerous researchers have derived M-polynomials for different indices (13). Early applications include the determination of Zagreb indices for infinite dendrimer nanostars14, the computation of M-polynomials for benzene rings embedded on P-type surfaces and polyhex nanotubes15, and the development of generalized M-polynomial forms for certain nanostructures16.
This NM–polynomial framework provides a unified and efficient way to calculate a wide variety of degree– and neighbourhood–based descriptors used in chemistry and QSPR/QSAR studies.

sec.title: Motivation
sec.p: The accurate prediction of physicochemical properties of drug-like molecules is critical for the rational design of therapeutic agents and biocompatible materials. Traditionally, researchers have explored simple mathematical relationships between topological indices and physicochemical properties, employing methods such as simple linear, multiple linear, quadratic, logarithmic, or cubic regressions. While these approaches provide initial insights, they often fall short in capturing the nonlinear and multivariate nature of molecular behavior, especially in structurally diverse compounds.

Moreover, many existing studies tend to focus on a narrow subset of drug classes, targeting specific diseases such as brain cancer, cardiovascular conditions, breast cancer, liver disorders, COVID-19, or emetic treatments. These focused datasets, while useful, limit the generalizability of models across broader structural or therapeutic classes.

In this context, we first evaluated a wide range of topological descriptors, including degree-based indices, distance-based indices, eccentricity-based indices, eigenvalue-based indices, and degree- as well as neighborhood-degree-based M-polynomial indices. Among these, the neighborhood-degree-based M-polynomial indices (NM-polynomial indices) exhibited superior predictive performance because they incorporate richer connectivity information than simple degree measures, making them more representative of the underlying molecular structure. By contrast, eigenvalue-based and eccentricity-based indices showed relatively weak performance. This comparative analysis guided our choice of NM-polynomial indices as the primary descriptors for our models.

To address the above limitations, the present work introduces a machine-learning-based framework for modeling the relationship between NM-polynomial indices and physicochemical properties of polycyclic drug structures. These structures encapsulate the diverse molecular architectures present in the aforementioned drug classes. By employing advanced regression models–including Linear, Ridge, Lasso, and ElasticNet regression–trained on 80% of the data and externally validated on the remaining 20%, we aim to build more robust and generalizable predictive models. This approach not only moves beyond simplistic functional forms but also captures deeper structural–property relationships applicable to a wide range of bioactive compounds.

sec.title: Material and methods
sec.p: In this section, we outline the methodology employed in this study to compute NM-Polynomial indices and analyze their correlation with physical characteristics of Mitoxantrone and Doxorubicin. The methodology is divided into two main phases: NM-Polynomial indices computation and statistical analysis.

sec.title: Computation of NM-polynomial indices
sec.p:
In Sect. 4, we compute the NM-Polynomial indices for Mitoxantrone and Doxorubicin using the following steps:
Graph Representation: The molecular structures of Mitoxantrone and Doxorubicin are transformed into molecular graphs, where atoms serve as vertices and chemical bonds as edges.
Graph Partitioning: The vertices and edges of the molecular graph are partitioned based on the neighborhood degree.
NM-Polynomial Indices Computation: NM-Polynomial indices are calculated, and graphical representations of the results are plotted using MATLAB software.

sec.title: Statistical analysis of NM-polynomial indices
sec.p: In Sect. 6, we perform a statistical analysis to investigate the relationship between NM-Polynomial indices and the physicochemical properties of polycyclic drug structures. The selected compounds represent a broad range of therapeutic categories, including anticancer, cardiovascular, emetic, hepatic, and antiviral agents.

Graph Representation and Index Computation. Each chemical compound was first transformed into a molecular graph, where atoms were treated as vertices and chemical bonds as edges. The adjacency matrix for each molecular graph was computed using the newGraph software31, which efficiently generates graph-theoretic representations of molecular structures.

To extract topological information, a Python-based algorithm was developed to compute a set of NM-polynomial indices from the adjacency matrices. These indices capture structural patterns and vertex connectivity of the molecular graph, providing predictive insights into the physicochemical behavior of the compounds.

Physicochemical Properties Collection. Relevant properties, including molar volume, surface tension, refractivity, polarizability, and boiling point, were obtained from trusted chemical databases such as PubChem32 and ChemSpider33 dated on 12 November 2025 . These properties served as target variables for predictive modeling.

Model Development and Validation. The dataset was split into 80% training and 20% external testing sets to ensure unbiased evaluation. All predictor variables were standardized using z-score normalization to account for scale differences. Four regression models–Linear, Ridge, Lasso, and ElasticNet–were applied to model the relationship between NM-polynomial indices (independent variables) and each physicochemical property (dependent variable).

Overall, this integrated methodology leverages molecular graph theory and machine learning to uncover complex, potentially nonlinear relationships between structural features and chemical properties of polycyclic drug structures, offering a generalizable and scalable predictive framework.

sec.title: Main results
sec.p: In this section, we are calculating the NM-polynomial indices for Doxorubicin and Mitoxantrone.

sec.title: Mitoxantrone
sec.p: Synthetic anthracycline antibiotic mitoxantrone is a powerful anticancer drug used to treat a variety of cancers, such as ovarian, breast, prostate, and non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma43. DNA binding and intercalation are made easier by its chemical structure, which consists of a planar, tricyclic aromatic ring system44. This special structure allows interactions with DNA and topoisomerase II45. It is composed of two benzene rings, a nitrogen-containing side chain, and a core quinone ring.

The advantages of mitoxantrone include its potent anticancer activity against a variety of cancers46, lower cardiotoxicity when compared to doxorubicin47, enhanced bioavailability because of lipophilicity48, and multitargeting potential49. Its drawbacks, however, include resistance development, hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression, and secondary cancers50.

Doxorubicin
sec.p: Doxorubicin, an anthracycline antibiotic derived from Streptomyces peucetius, has been a cornerstone of cancer treatment since its introduction in the 1960s34. It is used against a wide spectrum of malignancies, including breast, ovarian, bladder, and thyroid cancers; soft tissue and bone sarcomas; Hodgkin lymphoma; small-cell lung cancer; and acute lymphoblastic and myeloblastic leukemias35.

Despite its efficacy, the clinical use of doxorubicin is limited by unfavourable pharmacokinetics–high hydrophilicity, short half-life, low bioavailability, and a large volume of distribution–which contribute to dose-dependent adverse effects such as cardiotoxicity, extravasation, nephrotoxicity, myelosuppression, ovarian toxicity, and gonadotoxicity37,39. Its anticancer action involves DNA intercalation, topoisomerase II inhibition, and free-radical production, mediated by its amino group and quinone moiety36,40.

The mechanisms underlying tumour resistance to doxorubicin are distinct from its toxicity and are still not fully understood. Reported contributors include tumour-specific characteristics, alterations in drug efflux, disruption of apoptotic pathways, and genetic mutations41.

In parallel, to reduce off-target toxicity and improve delivery, researchers have investigated alternative formulations such as nanoparticles, liposomes, and polymeric micelles, as well as chemical modification of the parent molecule. Doxorubicin possesses two modifiable functional groups (–NH2 and –OH), which facilitate conjugation or hybridization with other anticancer pharmacophores; such modifications have shown promise in alleviating adverse effects rather than overcoming intrinsic tumour resistance42.

Overall, current research aims both to understand and circumvent tumour resistance mechanisms and to develop innovative doxorubicin derivatives or delivery systems that optimize therapeutic potential while minimizing toxicity.

sec.p: To compute the NM-polynomial indices for molecular graphs derived from chemical structures, we developed a Python-based algorithm using the NetworkX and NumPy libraries.

The adjacency matrix of each molecular graph is obtained using the newGraph software and provided as input to the code named NM_Polynomial_Indices.ipynb, which is available in the Supplementary Files.

This code offers a computationally efficient method for extracting a wide variety of NM-polynomial indices that can serve as graph-based features in cheminformatics and machine-learning models. The input can be easily adapted to other molecules by replacing the adjacency matrix string.

sec.title: Statistical analysis of NM-polynomial indices
sec.p: QSPR studies have become an essential methodology for predicting the physicochemical properties of molecules using NM-Polynomial indices. These indices, derived from molecular graphs, encapsulate structural information that correlates with the physicochemical characteristics of pharmaceutical compounds. The relationship between the physicochemical properties of polycyclic drug structures and their NM-Polynomial indices is an emerging area of research.

In this study, we consider nine NM-Polynomial indices (independent variables) and nine physicochemical properties (dependent variables) across a dataset of 45 polycyclic drug structures. Table 6 shows the PubChem CIDs and ChemSpider IDs of polycyclic drug structures. To compute the NM-Polynomial indices, the chemical structures of the compounds were first converted into molecular graphs. The calculated values of the NM-Polynomial indices are presented in Table 7 and while the physicochemical properties are detailed in Table 8.

To verify the generalizability of the developed models, both internal (cross-validation) and external validation strategies were employed. For internal validation, 5-fold cross-validation was implemented: the dataset was randomly divided into five equal subsets. In each iteration, four subsets were used for training the model, and the remaining subset was used for validation. This process was repeated five times so that each subset served as the validation set once. The average results and variation (SD and CI) provided a robust estimate of model performance and helped reduce overfitting.

sec.title: Applicability domain via Williams plots
sec.p: The Williams plot, shown in Figure 11, was employed to assess the applicability domain and reliability of the developed regression models for predicting various physicochemical properties. It presents standardized residuals versus leverage values for both training and external test sets. Most data points lie within the ±3 standardized residual limits (red dashed lines), indicating the absence of significant outliers. Likewise, the majority of compounds fall below the leverage threshold (green dashed line), suggesting limited influence on model performance. A few external test compounds are close to or slightly above this threshold, indicating that their predictions should be interpreted with caution.

Overall, the distribution of points in the Williams plots supports the robustness and generalizability of the models. Figure 11 includes results for boiling point, complexity, molar refractivity, flash point, polarization, enthalpy of vaporization, surface tension and molar volume. In all cases, most compounds remain within the acceptable limits, confirming that the predictions are reliable and the models are applicable to similar compounds within the studied chemical space.Figure 11
Williams Plots for seven physicochemical properties using appropriate regression models. Each plot shows standardized residuals versus leverage values for training and test sets.

sec.title: Discussion of results
sec.p:
The NM-polynomial indices encode not only the degree of each atom but also the degrees of its neighbouring atoms, thereby incorporating second-order connectivity information. This makes them sensitive to key structural features such as branching, ring size and fusion patterns, and heteroatom connectivity.
Branching and the presence of bulky substituents reduce intermolecular contact area and generally lower surface tension and molar volume, while also influencing volatility-related properties such as boiling point (BP), flash point (FP) and enthalpy of vaporisation (EoV).
Ring size and polycyclic frameworks increase molecular rigidity and packing efficiency; more rigid or compact molecules often show higher BP and EoV but lower molar volume compared with their open-chain analogues.
Heteroatom connectivity (oxygen, nitrogen, halogens, etc.) introduces polarity and hydrogen-bonding sites, which markedly affect BP, EoV, FP and surface tension by strengthening intermolecular forces. It also increases molar refractivity (MR) and polarizability (P) because these descriptors reflect the ease with which the electron cloud is distorted.
The combined pattern of branching, cyclicity and heteroatoms also contributes to the calculated complexity index, which mirrors the topological diversity of the molecule.Because NM-polynomial indices simultaneously encode these multiple layers of connectivity, they act as richer descriptors of the structural features that govern the studied physicochemical properties, explaining their stronger correlations and superior predictive performance compared with simpler degree-based indices.

This mixed performance suggests that while the proposed NM-polynomial indices can effectively capture structure-property relationships for some physicochemical properties, they may not contain sufficient information for others. The differences may stem from the inherent complexity of the properties, the limited sample size, or the diversity of the available compounds. Future work should therefore focus on enlarging the dataset, exploring additional or more informative descriptors, and testing alternative modeling strategies to improve the robustness and predictive power of the models across all properties.

sec.title: Correlation between NM-polynomial indices and physicochemical properties.
sec.p:
These findings confirm that while NM-polynomial indices provide strong structure-property signals for several physicochemical endpoints, their utility is property-dependent and may be limited for optical properties such as IoR. Future work could incorporate additional descriptors or hybrid models to improve predictions for these challenging properties.Figure 12

Comparative Analysis. From the above studies, it is evident that different indices and modeling techniques yield varying predictive strengths. Degree-based indices (Hui et al.) achieved moderate correlations, whereas irregularity indices (Ibtisam et al.) provided stronger correlations, with r values often exceeding 0.9. Entropy indices (Rauf et al.) showed relatively consistent but slightly lower correlations across multiple properties. Machine learning approaches (Kour & Sankar; Bayati et al.) demonstrated improved performance in several cases, even with small datasets, though the limited sample sizes may restrict generalizability. Overall, the evidence suggests that irregularity indices and machine learning-based models generally provide more accurate predictive relationships than traditional degree-based or entropy-based indices.

Proposed Work. In this study, we introduce machine learning models based on newly defined NM polynomial indices for predicting physicochemical properties of polycyclic drug structures. Unlike earlier works, which relied on small datasets of 13-18 drug structures, our analysis considers a substantially larger dataset of 45 drug structures, leading to improved generalization of the results. In addition, we employed both cross-validation (CV) and external validation procedures, ensuring more robust and unbiased estimates of predictive performance compared to the simple regression or single-split validations used in prior studies.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: NM-polynomial indices play a crucial role in predicting the physical and chemical properties of drug compounds. In this study, we computed NM-polynomial indices for Mitoxantrone and Doxorubicin and analyzed their effectiveness in QSPR investigations. The numerical results confirmed that NM-polynomial indices provide valuable insights into the molecular characteristics of drugs. By integrating graph-theoretic measures with machine learning regression models (Linear, Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net), and validating the models through cross-validation (CV), external testing, and confidence interval (CI) analysis, we established significant structure-property relationships for the majority of the investigated attributes.

Based on the analysis of NM-polynomial indices with various physicochemical properties using multiple machine learning models, the following conclusions can be drawn:
The NM-polynomial indices exhibited strong and statistically significant correlations with most of the studied physicochemical properties, including complexity, boiling point, enthalpy of vaporization, flash point, molar refractivity, polarizability, surface tension, and molar volume.
The predictive performance of the models indicates that NM-polynomial indices are effective descriptors for modeling and estimating the majority of physicochemical properties of the studied compounds. Across multiple regression models, particularly Ridge and Elastic Net, the predictive accuracy for these properties was consistently high, reinforcing the robustness of NM-polynomial indices as predictors in QSAR/QSPR modeling.
Ridge and Elastic Net regression models generally outperformed Linear and Lasso regression, highlighting the importance of regularization when modeling these properties.
Limitation. One physicochemical property–index of refraction–did not exhibit statistically significant correlations with NM-polynomial indices. This indicates that the index of refraction may be influenced by structural or functional molecular features not fully captured within the NM-polynomial framework. To address this limitation, future work may explore hybrid models that integrate NM-polynomial indices with complementary descriptors, such as quantum chemical parameters or three-dimensional molecular shape descriptors, to enhance predictive performance for such less-correlated properties.Overall, the findings confirm the predictive power of NM-polynomial indices for a broad range of physicochemical attributes, while also identifying specific areas where the approach could be enhanced to address its current limitations.
